Let’s dive into Chapter 9: Overcoming Common Barriers—Practical Strategies for Sticky Communication.
Even if you’ve got a solid framework, real-world communication has its fair share of roadblocks. People are busy, they’re skeptical, and honestly, they’re more distracted than ever. If you want your ideas to really stick, you’ve got to see these barriers coming—and know how to handle them.
One of the biggest hurdles is what’s called the curse of knowledge. Ever found yourself assuming someone just gets what you’re saying—because it seems obvious to you? That’s the curse at work. The key to overcoming it is to step out of your own shoes and really look at things from your listener’s perspective. That means simplifying your language, using down-to-earth examples, and most importantly, testing your message with real people to see what actually lands.
Now, let’s talk about information overload. We live in a world that’s noisy and full of distractions. Only the clearest, most compelling messages actually break through. That’s why sticking to the core idea—and presenting it in a way that’s unexpected—can make all the difference. When you focus on what truly matters and deliver it with a bit of surprise, you’ll stand out from all that background noise.
What about skepticism? People are naturally wary of big promises and slick tactics. The antidote? Be honest and transparent. Instead of pushing, invite your audience to test your ideas for themselves. When you build credibility this way, trust follows.
So, how do you put this into practice? Here are a few tried-and-true strategies:
First, test your messages with real audiences. Get their feedback—listen for what sticks, and don’t be afraid to tweak your message so it resonates even more.
Second, use analogies and stories. They turn abstract ideas into something people can relate to—and remember.
And third, focus on action. Be clear about what steps people can actually take. Vague advice won’t move anyone.
Think about a company launching a new product. Instead of rolling out a massive campaign right away, they might run a small pilot first—trying out different messages, watching to see which ones people remember or act on. With those real-world insights, they can refine their approach and scale up with confidence.
In the end, sticky communication isn’t something you just master once and for all. It’s an ongoing process—one that’s all about learning, adapting, and staying curious. By welcoming feedback and staying open to what really works, you’ll keep getting better at crafting messages that truly endure.
